tagline.text: A hilltop of rock with a hole through it, on the coast north of Pagudpud

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May (at low tide, on days with gentle waves)

children.text: Bantay Abot Cave is a rocky hill on the Balaoi coast north of Pagudpud, with a hole through its middle that frames the sea like a picture. Despite the name, it is closer to a natural arch than a cave, and it makes a quick stop on the northern Pagudpud route.

Bantay Abot Cave sits on the coast of Barangay Balaoi in Pagudpud, Ilocos Norte. Pagudpud is a beach town at the very northern tip of Luzon, and this stretch is a rocky shore facing the South China Sea. English Wikipedia describes the site as a rock archway framing a rocky shoreline, while the municipal guide places it in Sitio Gaoa. On maps it shows up as a viewpoint near the Balaoi–Aryargo Road.

The name can be read in Ilocano. Bantay is said to mean mountain and abot hole, so the name translates as "mountain with a hole," which is also how English Wikipedia renders it. So if the word "cave" makes you expect a deep, dark tunnel, adjust your expectations. It is not a cave that runs far inside. It is a rocky hill with a large opening through it, and you look out through that opening to the sea. Go with the right expectations and you will enjoy it much more.

There are stories about how the hill came to look this way. Wikipedia says it is believed to have been a hill eroded after an earthquake, and travel blogs and reviews mention that part of the arch collapsed in an earthquake in the 1980s. The year and the details differ from source to source, so they cannot be treated as settled fact. What is clear is that waves still keep carving the rock, and that the green vegetation on top and the bare rock below make a strong contrast of color.

Timmangtang Rock is worth knowing about too. Of the two rocks, it is the first one you see from the national road on the way to Blue Lagoon or Maira-ira Beach, and its green cover has been compared to the shell of a giant sea turtle. Bantay Abot Cave is not visible from the road and is tucked away below a staircase, so when Timmangtang Rock comes into view, stop nearby and look for the steps down to the cave. Some visitors climb Timmangtang Rock to photograph the cave from a distance, but the rock can be slippery, so do not push your luck. Keep in mind how short a visit is, too. One reviewer arrived at around 5:30 PM and stayed 14 minutes. Walking down the stairs, crossing the rocky shore, taking photos and climbing back usually takes about 30 minutes, or about an hour if the tide is right and you take your time. So rather than coming a long way for this alone, it fits best as one stop on a day tour of the northern Pagudpud coast.
The opening through the hill works as a frame. Photos come out well both from inside the opening looking out to sea and from the seaward side looking back at the shape of the rock.
The top of the rock is covered in green vegetation while the base is bare rock washed by waves. On a clear day, with the blue-green water, it is known as a photo spot.

blocks.title: A rocky shore at low tide

children.text: Going down the roadside stairs, you cross an uneven rocky shore to reach the arch. Visitors who came at low tide said access was good, and some reviews mention seeing small fish and large crabs in the water.

blocks.title: Timmangtang Rock and the Lover's Rock legend

children.text: Local lore pairs the nearby Timmangtang Rock with this one, and together the two rocks are sometimes called the Lover's Rock. They are said to be about
apart.

There is parking by the side of the road on the right, and you can simply follow the signs. With no long hike, families with children and groups with members who find walking hard can choose a viewing spot and still enjoy it.

blocks.title: A stop on the northern Pagudpud route

children.text: Kabigan Falls, the Patapat Viaduct and Blue Lagoon lie in the same direction, and the cave is often included in the tricycle tour. It makes a good spot to rest and look at the sea between them.

items.title: Northern tricycle tour
items.subtitle: From Kabigan Falls to Blue Lagoon

children.text: Find a tricycle in Pagudpud town or at a Saud Beach resort. Agree on the fare, the stops included and the waiting time before you leave.
Visiting Kabigan Falls first lets you walk during the cooler morning hours.
On the way back from the falls, stop at Bantay Abot Cave, walk down the stairs and look at the sea through the hole. Check the tide and the waves first.
Take photos and have lunch by the roadside where Timmangtang Rock comes into view.
Continue to the Patapat Viaduct and Blue Lagoon.
You can change the order. On days with rough waves, though, it is safer to skip the rocky shore section and be content with the roadside view.

From Laoag, take the Pan-Philippine Highway north and turn left at the Balaoi police outpost. The road leads toward the beach resorts, and you will see signs for Bantay Abot Cave along the way.
There is space to park on the right side of the road.
Take a tricycle from Pagudpud town or Saud Beach. The northern tour is known to cost about

The cave is not visible from the road. You have to go down a concrete staircase by the roadside and cross a rocky stretch of shore.

The best time to travel is November–May, and the dry season starts from December. Because this is an outdoor rocky shore, waves and tides matter more than the weather in deciding whether a visit works.
Many reviewers say it is safer to go at low tide. Municipal-type guidance also advises checking conditions on the day, since access can change with the weather, the tide and the waves.

During the day, morning or the late afternoon as the sun gets lower is best for photos and less hot. At midday the rocky shore has almost no shade and the glare is strong, so bring a hat and sunscreen. One reviewer arrived in the late afternoon and had only a short look around. Once the sun sets, though, it is hard to see where you are stepping on the rocks, so it is safer to be back before dark.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Northeast monsoon, high waves and relatively cool
Check first whether waves reach the rocky shore section, and do not push your luck.
Visibility is good and photos come out well, but there is little shade at midday, so bring a hat and water.
Rocks are wet and slippery and waves may be high, so postpone the visit or settle for a view from a distance.

There is not much lodging right next to the cave, so the usual approach is to stay in Pagudpud town or near Saud Beach and go by tricycle. Hannah's Beach Resort appears in reviews as a nearby beach resort, about 5 minutes by car from here. If your lodging introduces a tricycle driver, it is easier to get a clear fare.

For meals, eat in Pagudpud town or at a beach resort. Around the cave there are only simple snacks, so bring water and snacks with you, and since ATMs are scarce in the beach areas, withdraw plenty of cash in Laoag. Most small shops accept cash only.

When planning a day that includes Bantay Abot Cave, it helps to decide where to have lunch first. If you have been to Kabigan Falls, a sensible flow is to see the cave, return to Pagudpud town or the Saud Beach area for a meal, and head to Blue Lagoon in the afternoon. Restaurants and lodgings sometimes close depending on the season and operating conditions, so check just before you go.
Go at low tide so that the rocky shore is easy to cross. At high tide the rocks can be covered by waves or wet.
The rocks are slippery and sharp. One reviewer had to be careful even in trekking sandals, so wear non-slip shoes that leave your hands free.
Keep your camera and phone in a waterproof pouch, and put them in your bag on rough sections so that both hands are free.
It is a windy spot, so take care that hats and light items do not blow away.
Try both views: the sea seen from inside the opening and the rock seen from the sea side.
Tell your tricycle driver in advance that you want to stay long enough for photos, and you will not feel rushed.
If someone in your group finds walking difficult, let them know beforehand and have them wait at the roadside viewpoint.
Take your trash with you, and do not touch or take rocks or shore life.
Low tide does not always mean it is safe. If waves reach the approach or the rocks are wet, do not go close, and view the arch from a distance.
The approach consists of stairs and an uneven rocky shore, and you can get wet or fall when waves come in.
Follow any signs or local instructions that restrict access.
Always keep your way back clear and return before sunset. Near dusk it is hard to see the rocks.
If you have children with you, hold their hands on the rocky shore section.
Entrance fees and operations can change, so check the latest notices with the Pagudpud tourism office or your lodging before you go.
